newsitem.title: USA: American, pilots, both upbeat, set for fresh talks.
newsitem.headline: American, pilots, both upbeat, set for fresh talks.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots Tuesday cited progress in talks to settle the dispute that sparked a brief strike last month, and the airline said a deal could be reached by Friday.

James Sovich, president of the Allied Pilots Association, told union members in a recorded telephone message that weekend talks with the nation's second-largest airline were productive and negotations would resume in Washington on Wednesday.
American also called the talks productive and said it expected a tentative settlement by Friday, in time for a scheduled meeting of the union's board of directors.

Fort Worth, Tex.-based American and its pilots union resumed talks Friday for the first time since a week of intensive negotiations broke down without an agreement Feb. 14, sparking a brief strike by the 9,300-member union.

President Clinton immediately stepped in and created an emergency board to try to resolve the dispute, which is over wages and who will fly new smaller jets at American's regional carrier, American Eagle. His action halted the strike.
Clinton on Monday extended the deadline for a report from Presidential Emergency Board Chairman Robert Harris, who said the extra days could help to resolve the dispute.
"I anticipate bargaining will continue until the APA board of directors meets in Washington on Friday," Sovich said.
"The endgame in the process is an acceptable negotiated settlement. We will leave no stone unturned in our efforts to secure a contract for our pilots."

Under federal labor law governing airlines, Clinton's action stopped the pilots from striking and stopped American from locking the pilots out for 60 days while the board drew up a proposed settlement and the two sides considered it.

American and the union also agreed on Monday to extend the 60-day period to April 28, two weeks beyond the original deadline. If a settlement is not reached by April 28, the pilots could strike or American could lock them out.

If the union's 9,300 pilots strike, only Congress could end the walkout by passing a law ordering them back to work and requiring them to accept the presidential board's settlement or enter into arbitration.
At issue in the talks are wages and work rules.
On wages, the union wants an 11 percent increase to cover the last three years, when it got no raises, and the next four. American has offered 6.5 percent.

The union also wants its members, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, in the cockpits of the new smaller jets. But American says it cannot compete with other commuter carriers unless the new jets are flown by the lower-paid American Eagle pilots.
